problem: Prompt injection has been studied for text and web LLM applications, but not for LLM-based navigation agents. These agents are black-box, take long contexts that dilute injected text, and output executable plans rather than plain text, so existing injection attacks are weak on them.
motivation: A successful injection on a navigation agent can misguide physical movement and cause unsafe routes or mission failure, not just wrong text. Existing hand-crafted injections (naive, escape, ignore, combined) achieve limited ASR on navigation agents, so attacks must be optimized with navigation-specific feedback.
key_idea: Iteratively optimize an injection prompt offline on a surrogate navigation agent, using an aggregated navigation-metric attack score plus KL-divergence and key-token signals from a surrogate LLM, turned into textual feedback (TextGrad-style) to refine the prompt.
insight: Combining task-level metrics with distribution-level signals gives finer guidance than task-level score alone. In the ablation on NavGPT (GPT-3.5), removing the Distribution Analyzer lowers ASR from 75.00% to 69.25%, and either KL or key-token alone gives 72.90% with weaker SPL/nDTW degradation. A prompt optimized on NavGPT with GPT-3.5 transfers to GPT-4 and to an outdoor agent, which the authors attribute to the metric aggregation, though transfer is only tested on a few agents.
method: Attack Evaluator: runs the surrogate navigation agent (NavGPT, GPT-3.5) with the injected instruction and computes S = w^T M_nav, a weighted sum (weights sum to 1) of TL, NE, SR and quality indicators such as SPL.
Distribution Analyzer (KL): with a surrogate LLM (Llama2-7b), computes average token-level KL divergence between the attacked and original instruction distributions.
Distribution Analyzer (key tokens): per-position score |ΔPmax|+|ΔEntropy|; tokens above a threshold τ_token are key tokens. Combined into D = αKL + (1-α)·mean key-token score, with α=0.5.

Adaptive Prompt Refinement: a Feedback Generator converts S, D and key tokens into textual suggestions (keep high-impact tokens, replace ineffective words, insert distractors, reorder phrases); a Prompt Updater rewrites the prompt.
Optimization loop: for R rounds, evaluate, keep the best prompt, and stop early if S ≥ τ. Optimization uses 100 random R2R instructions.
Threat model: black-box, the attacker injects text into external input channels and optimizes offline on a surrogate simulator, then applies the prompt to the target.

setting.backbone: Attack optimization uses NavGPT (GPT-3.5-turbo) as evaluator and Llama2-7b as surrogate LLM. Victims are NavGPT (GPT-3.5 / GPT-4) and the Balcı et al. LLM UAV agent, all frozen and black-box.
setting.training_data: No model training. Prompt optimization uses 100 random R2R instructions.
setting.observation: Text instruction injection into a navigation agent whose observations are textual descriptions (NavGPT on R2R panoramas) or a UAV outdoor agent.
setting.action_space: Attack acts on the instruction text. Victim actions are discrete nav-graph viewpoints (NavGPT) or flight commands (outdoor agent).
setting.simulator: Matterport3D / R2R (NavGPT); an outdoor UAV simulator for the Balcı agent
setting.privileged: Access to a surrogate simulator matching the target's architecture and I/O format (surrogate, not the target itself); otherwise none.

Adaptive-defense (self-reminder) row: ASR 68.80, TL 6.13, NE 8.59, SPL 5.49, nDTW 36.08, CLS 38.04 (NavGPT GPT-3.5). Ablation variants are in Tab. 2.
results: PINA reaches ASR 75% on NavGPT (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4) and 100% on the outdoor agent. The strongest baseline, Combined Attack, gets 50% on NavGPT (both LLMs) and 84.21% on the outdoor agent. On NavGPT with GPT-3.5, SPL falls from 14.30 to 3.56. Under a self-reminder defense ASR drops only to 68.80%.
limitations: Only three victim configurations are tested (NavGPT with GPT-3.5/GPT-4 and one outdoor agent), and only a simple self-reminder defense is evaluated.

Assumes a surrogate simulator that matches the target's architecture and I/O, and the evaluation set sizes are not reported. The outdoor ASR of 100% is trivially inflated because the clean agent has NE=0.
Simulation only, with no real-robot tests, and the outdoor benchmark is not standard.
builds_on: Formalizing and Benchmarking Prompt Injection Attacks (Liu et al.)
